distillation_scope: Pure disease-name leaf distillation for the full clinical spectrum of brucellosis.

latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Entry through unpasteurized dairy ingestion, occupational livestock exposure, laboratory aerosol, conjunctival inoculation, or skin breaks. This is the upstream prior gate, not a disease-course severity marker by itself.

Brucella survives in macrophages by avoiding phagolysosomal killing and replicates in reticuloendothelial cells; this intracellular niche explains chronicity, relapse risk, and need for prolonged intracellular-active combination therapy.

Hematogenous and macrophage-mediated spread to liver, spleen, bone marrow, lymph nodes, spine, CNS, heart valves, and genitourinary tissues. Drives hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias, bacteremia, and focal organ disease.

TNF, IL-1, IL-6, and interferon-gamma response to intracellular infection produces undulant fever, rigors, drenching sweats, malaise, weight loss, myalgia, arthralgia, and acute-phase reactant elevation. Inflammation is often less pyogenic than ordinary gram-negative sepsis.

Cell-mediated containment produces granulomatous lesions and sometimes suppurative microabscesses in liver, spleen, bone marrow, spine, CNS, and other organs; responsible for focal brucellosis and prolonged symptoms.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Bone marrow and hypersplenic cytopenia pathway
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Marrow infection, granulomatous infiltration, hemophagocytic-like activation, and splenic sequestration can produce anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, or pancytopenia; cytopenias are usually reversible with antimicrobial therapy.

Hematogenous seeding of sacroiliac joints, lumbar vertebral endplates, discs, paraspinal tissues, and large joints. Produces sacroiliitis, spondylitis, spondylodiscitis, epidural/paraspinal/psoas abscess, chronic back pain, and radiculopathy.

Brucella reaches meninges, brain parenchyma, cranial nerves, spinal cord, or cerebral vessels, causing lymphocytic meningitis, encephalitis, cranial neuropathy, seizures, granulomas, stroke-like vasculitis, hearing loss, or myelopathy.

Persistent bacteremia seeds native valves, prosthetic valves, cardiac devices, or aneurysmal vascular tissue. Rare, but it is the dominant direct mortality pathway in brucellosis because of destructive valve disease, heart failure, embolization, and mycotic aneurysm.

Reticuloendothelial infection in liver and spleen produces hepatosplenomegaly, cholestatic or mild hepatitic enzyme elevation, hypodense splenic or hepatic lesions, and rare chronic suppurative abscesses that may require drainage.
Hematogenous seeding of epididymis, testis, prostate, kidney, or urinary tract produces epididymo-orchitis, testicular abscess, prostatitis, or sterile urinary symptoms in a minority of patients.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: After mucosal or occupational exposure, viable Brucella establish intracellular infection after a variable incubation period.
Surviving macrophage-associated organisms disseminate through blood and reticuloendothelial organs.
Intracellular burden drives constitutional symptoms and acute-phase response.
Disseminated organisms in macrophage-rich organs induce granulomatous containment and focal lesions.
Bone marrow involvement and splenic sequestration explain anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and pancytopenia.
Hematogenous spread commonly seeds sacroiliac joints and lumbar spine.
Persistent bacteremia and intracellular dissemination occasionally involve meninges, CNS parenchyma, cranial nerves, or vessels.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Amplified by prosthetic valves, cardiac implantable electronic devices, native valvular disease, aneurysm, or prolonged untreated bacteremia.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Endovascular seeding is rare but lethal and requires distinct treatment and source-control decisions.
Liver and spleen are macrophage-rich target organs for granuloma and abscess formation.
Fever is the most common systemic manifestation and may be intermittent or undulant.
A prolonged fever history is more informative than a single normal triage temperature in subacute brucellosis.
Persistence of intracellular burden creates recurring fever peaks rather than a single monophasic febrile illness.
Drenching and sometimes malodorous sweats are a classic systemic clue.
Rigors may accompany bacteremic fever spikes.
Malaise and fatigue reflect systemic cytokine activity and can persist for months.
Chronic fever, anorexia, and inflammation produce weight loss in delayed presentations.
CRP is variably elevated; very high values suggest focal abscess, endocarditis, or severe inflammatory burden.
ESR often rises in chronic and osteoarticular brucellosis.
Anemia of inflammation, marrow involvement, and hypersplenism can lower hemoglobin.
Leukopenia is common, although focal abscess or severe bacterial inflammation can instead cause leukocytosis.
Thrombocytopenia can arise from marrow involvement, hypersplenism, or immune consumption.
Splenic reticuloendothelial infection and congestion produce splenomegaly.
Suppurative hepatosplenic brucellosis produces hypodense abscess lesions that often need drainage plus prolonged therapy.
Hepatic reticuloendothelial involvement can enlarge the liver.
Mild transaminitis may accompany hepatic granulomatous involvement.
Lumbar spondylitis/sacroiliitis presents with persistent low back pain.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Requires nerve-root irritation from spondylodiscitis, epidural extension, paraspinal abscess, or foraminal inflammation.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Radicular pain and paresthesias signal spinal extension beyond uncomplicated arthralgia.
Spine is the most serious osteoarticular target; MRI shows vertebral/disc inflammation and adjacent soft-tissue extension.
Osteoarticular seeding is common enough to model as a disease-course event hazard.
CNS mechanism manifests as meningitis, encephalitis, cranial neuropathy, stroke-like vasculitis, or myelopathy.
Headache is common with neurobrucellosis and meningitis.
CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis is a typical neurobrucellosis pattern.
Basal meningitis and inflammatory blood-CSF barrier injury raise CSF protein.
Low CSF glucose can mimic tuberculous meningitis in neurobrucellosis.
Granulomas, encephalitis, infarction, and meningeal irritation can precipitate seizures.
Endocarditis is rare but accounts for a disproportionate share of brucellosis deaths.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Amplified by short-course therapy, monotherapy, poor adherence, inadequate intracellular coverage, or undrained focal disease.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Relapse reflects residual intracellular organisms or persistent focal niches.
Biopsy or aspirate culture from a focal abscess, vertebral/disc site, or tissue lesion can directly recover Brucella when blood culture is negative or delayed.
Valve destruction, heart failure, emboli, device infection, and mycotic aneurysm are the main direct death pathway.
CNS vasculitis, hydrocephalus, seizures, or myelopathy can be fatal or disabling without prolonged CNS-penetrating therapy.
Large hepatosplenic abscesses persist despite antibiotics and may require drainage.

axes.shape_free_text: Any credible Brucella exposure: unpasteurized dairy, livestock or abattoir work, veterinary/lab exposure, endemic-area residence/travel, or hunting/feral animal contact.
Consumption of unpasteurized milk, cheese, or camel/goat/sheep dairy before illness.
Occupational or household contact with goats, sheep, cattle, camels, pigs, animal birth products, abattoir material, or veterinary specimens.
Residence in or travel from an endemic region within the incubation or chronic symptom window.
Can be normal at a single visit or rise to 38-40.5 degC during febrile waves; prolonged/undulant course is more characteristic than the exact snapshot value.
Prolonged fever history over days to months, often intermittent.
Recurrent fever waves with relative defervescence between peaks; more common in subacute or untreated illness.
Usually tracks fever and dehydration; marked tachycardia suggests severe systemic illness, abscess, endocarditis, or shock physiology.
Usually normal to mildly elevated; tachypnea rises with sepsis physiology, pleural involvement, metabolic acidosis, or severe focal disease.
Typically preserved; low systolic pressure indicates dehydration, sepsis physiology, hemorrhage, endocarditis heart failure, or another complication.
Usually normal; falls with severe focal infection, dehydration, sepsis physiology, or endocarditis complications.
Chills or shaking rigors with fever spikes.
Drenching nocturnal sweats, sometimes described as malodorous, often accompanying subacute disease.
Malaise, exhaustion, asthenia, reduced activity, and slow recovery.
Unintentional weight loss from prolonged fever and anorexia.
Diffuse muscle pain as part of systemic brucellosis.
Diffuse arthralgia without requiring objective arthritis; common in systemic brucellosis.
Persistent lumbar or sacroiliac pain; focal severity rises with sacroiliitis, spondylitis, or spondylodiscitis.
Shooting leg pain, paresthesia, numbness, or root-distribution symptoms from spinal inflammation or abscess.
General systemic headache or prominent neurobrucellosis headache.
Nausea or vomiting from systemic infection, CNS involvement, hepatic involvement, or drug intolerance.
Diffuse or focal abdominal pain from hepatosplenic involvement, abscess, or systemic illness.
Left hypochondrial or left upper quadrant pain/tenderness, especially with splenomegaly or splenic abscess.
Palpable or imaging hepatomegaly from reticuloendothelial involvement.
Palpable, percussion, ultrasound, or CT splenomegaly.
Clinically or radiographically abnormal lymphadenopathy; may occur but is not required.
Normal or low in uncomplicated disease; leukocytosis can occur with focal abscess, severe inflammation, or another process.
Usually normal or mildly reduced; high neutrophilia suggests suppurative focal disease or co-infection.
Mild anemia from chronic inflammation, marrow involvement, or hypersplenism.
Normal to low; thrombocytopenia is usually mild but pancytopenia can occur.
Often elevated in subacute, chronic, osteoarticular, or focal brucellosis; can be low early or in some neurobrucellosis cases.
Usually mild to moderate elevation; marked elevation favors abscess, spondylodiscitis, endocarditis, or severe systemic illness.
Normal to mildly elevated; substantial elevation suggests hepatic focal disease, co-infection, drug injury, or another diagnosis.
Normal to mildly elevated hepatitic component.
May rise with hepatic granulomatous or cholestatic involvement.
Usually normal; rises with dehydration, severe systemic illness, renal focal disease, or aminoglycoside toxicity.
May rise with dehydration, AKI, or severe systemic illness.
Can be low with chronic inflammation, poor intake, SIADH-like physiology, or CNS disease.
Usually normal; low values reflect dehydration, renal dysfunction, or sepsis physiology.
Blood culture confirmation probability; sensitivity varies with disease phase, prior antibiotics, incubation duration, and lab notification.
Culture positivity from abscess aspirate, vertebral/disc biopsy, tissue biopsy, or other focal lesion; especially relevant in focal brucellosis.
Rose Bengal, standard tube agglutination, Coombs, 2ME, or Brucella IgM/IgG activity. Can be negative early or in neurobrucellosis; repeat testing may convert.
Brucella DNA detection in blood, tissue, or CSF when available; useful when cultures or serology are negative but availability varies.
MRI/CT evidence of brucellar spondylitis, discitis, or spondylodiscitis, often lumbar and sometimes with paraspinal extension.
Paraspinal, psoas, piriformis, gluteal, or intramuscular abscess associated with spinal brucellosis.
Spinal epidural abscess or epidural inflammatory extension related to brucellar spondylodiscitis.
CNS or peripheral nervous system involvement: meningitis, meningoencephalitis, cranial neuropathy, vasculitis, granuloma, seizure, myelitis, radiculitis, or hearing loss.
Meningismus can be subtle or absent despite abnormal CSF.
Cranial nerve involvement including abducens, facial, vestibulocochlear, or optic pathways.
Generalized or focal seizures with neurobrucellosis, granuloma, encephalitis, or vasculitic infarction.
Focal motor deficit from neurobrucellosis vasculitis, infarction, granuloma, or spinal cord involvement.
CSF pleocytosis, typically lymphocytic and often tens to hundreds of cells/uL.
Lymphocyte predominance in CSF; neutrophilic early presentations can occur but lymphocytic pattern is typical.
Elevated CSF protein from meningeal inflammation and barrier dysfunction.
Low or low-normal CSF glucose; can closely mimic tuberculous meningitis.
Ultrasound/CT hypodense or fluid collection in spleen attributable to brucellosis.
Largest diameter of a splenic abscess lesion; larger or persistent lesions increase source-control need.
Pleural effusion can occur with systemic brucellosis, hepatosplenic abscess, endocarditis, or alternative diagnoses; not specific.
Rare event hazard, strongly increased by valvular disease, prosthetic valve, cardiac device, aneurysm, or delayed treatment; major driver of disease mortality.
Hazard of clinically meaningful spinal brucellosis; rises with delayed diagnosis and persistent bacteremia.
Hazard of CNS/PNS involvement; uncommon but clinically important because it changes treatment duration and CNS-penetrating coverage.
Hazard of hepatosplenic suppurative abscess, especially in chronic or relapsed disease.
Hazard of new neurologic compromise from epidural abscess or spinal inflammatory compression.
Post-treatment relapse hazard from inadequate regimen, poor adherence, persistent focal disease, immunosuppression, or source-control failure.
Need for drainage, device extraction, valve surgery, abscess evacuation, or decompression beyond antimicrobials.
Probability the selected regimen contains effective intracellular-active Brucella therapy with adequate duration and combination coverage.
Pregnancy changes regimen selection because tetracyclines and some alternatives are avoided and fetal loss risk is clinically relevant.
Baseline liver disease, transaminitis, cholestasis, or critical drug interactions that reduce rifampin feasibility or require monitoring.
Risk of nephrotoxicity or ototoxicity from gentamicin/streptomycin, increased by renal impairment, older age, dehydration, or baseline hearing/vestibular disease.

Overall mortality is low with prompt treatment, but hazard rises with endocarditis, aortic/mycotic aneurysm, severe neurobrucellosis, uncontrolled abscess, delayed diagnosis, or severe host vulnerability.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Fever and sympathetic activation increase heart rate; discordance suggests dehydration, drugs, conduction disease, or endocarditis.
Both are constitutional outputs of the same cytokine mechanism; neither should directly cause the other.
Persistent fever and anorexia create delayed weight loss in subacute/chronic disease.
Hypersplenism can contribute to thrombocytopenia in reticuloendothelial disease.
Splenic capsular inflammation and perisplenic fat stranding produce left upper quadrant pain.
Large or persistent splenic abscess often needs drainage plus antibiotics.
Vertebral and disc inflammation produce persistent focal back pain.
Epidural extension can compress roots or cord and increases urgency of surgical assessment.
Neurobrucellosis gates interpretation of CSF pleocytosis as disease-relevant rather than incidental.
Basal meningitis pattern can lower CSF glucose.
CNS granuloma, vasculitis, or encephalitis can trigger seizures.
Endocarditis, prosthetic valve infection, or device infection is the major brucellosis mortality driver.
Undrained abscess, retained infected device, or uncorrected valve focus sustains intracellular infection and relapse.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Doxycycline is generally avoided in pregnancy; regimen selection shifts to pregnancy-compatible alternatives.
Rifampin can worsen liver injury and has major drug interactions.
Antibiotics alone may fail when there is a drainable abscess, infected valve/device, or compressive spinal abscess.

failure_modes: poor adherence to prolonged dual therapy
unrecognized focal disease requiring longer therapy or source control
rifampin drug interaction reducing efficacy of a co-medication or causing discontinuation
treatments.context_specific_role: Core oral intracellular-active combination for uncomplicated systemic brucellosis when pregnancy and major rifampin constraints are absent.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Renal impairment, dehydration, or baseline otovestibular disease makes gentamicin/streptomycin less usable.

failure_modes: aminoglycoside stopped early because of nephrotoxicity
monotherapy after initial aminoglycoside without adequate oral companion
unrecognized CNS disease where aminoglycoside penetration is inadequate
treatments.context_specific_role: Bactericidal combination option, especially when rapid burden reduction or relapse prevention is important and renal/otovestibular risk is acceptable.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Spinal brucellosis often needs prolonged multi-drug therapy to reduce relapse and neurologic complications.
Endovascular disease requires aggressive combination therapy in parallel with surgical/device evaluation.
Renal or otovestibular risk may force aminoglycoside avoidance or early substitution.

failure_modes: source-control need ignored
toxicity limits aminoglycoside completion
therapy duration too short for focal disease
treatments.context_specific_role: Escalated antimicrobial path for complicated focal disease such as spondylodiscitis or suspected endovascular involvement when toxicity constraints allow.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Ceftriaxone adds CSF-active bactericidal coverage while doxycycline/rifampin provide intracellular activity.
Doxycycline component is generally avoided in pregnancy.

failure_modes: stopping therapy before CSF and neurologic response normalize
missing obstructive hydrocephalus, abscess, or stroke complication
drug intolerance limiting prolonged therapy

side_effects.interpretation: Hepatic monitoring during prolonged combination treatment.

treatments.context_specific_role: CNS-penetrating antimicrobial path for neurobrucellosis, typically requiring prolonged therapy and serial neurologic/CSF assessment.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: TMP-SMX has CNS penetration and is commonly part of prolonged neurobrucellosis combinations.
Folate antagonism and late-pregnancy neonatal risks require obstetric infectious disease review.

failure_modes: used alone instead of in combination
cytopenia or renal adverse effects requiring discontinuation
insufficient duration for neurobrucellosis

side_effects.interpretation: Creatinine rise from tubular secretion effect or true renal injury.

treatments.context_specific_role: Add-on or alternative companion for neurobrucellosis, pediatric/pregnancy-constrained scenarios, relapse, or intolerance to standard agents.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Fluoroquinolone may substitute when aminoglycoside toxicity forces discontinuation, but should remain part of combination therapy.
Fluoroquinolones are generally avoided in pregnancy.

failure_modes: used as inadequate monotherapy
tendinopathy/QT/CNS adverse effects
resistance or poor activity compared with standard combination

side_effects.interpretation: Rare CNS adverse effect, higher in predisposed patients.

treatments.context_specific_role: Substitution component when standard agents cannot be used or toxicity requires switching.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Drainage or decompression directly removes a persistent niche that antibiotics penetrate poorly.
Neurologic compromise changes source control from elective to urgent.

failure_modes: lesion not technically drainable
drainage without adequate antimicrobial therapy
missed additional focal sites
treatments.context_specific_role: Source control for splenic/hepatic/psoas/paraspinal abscess or compressive spinal disease.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Destructive valve infection or infected hardware often cannot be sterilized reliably without removal/repair.

failure_modes: patient too unstable or high-risk for surgery
device retained despite persistent infection
antimicrobial course too short after source control

side_effects.interpretation: Perioperative hazard exists but can be outweighed by endovascular source control.

treatments.context_specific_role: Endovascular source control for valve destruction, prosthetic valve disease, cardiac device infection, or infected aneurysm.

exposure_prior.trajectory_modulation: Strongly increases pre-test probability and explains gastrointestinal/mucosal acquisition.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Unpasteurized milk or cheese is a major Brucella exposure route.

exposure_prior.trajectory_modulation: Raises probability of occupational inoculation or aerosol exposure.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Livestock, veterinary, abattoir, dairy, and laboratory work are classic Brucella exposure contexts.

exposure_prior.trajectory_modulation: Supports brucellosis when fever, sweats, back pain, cytopenia, or focal disease otherwise appears nonspecific.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Brucellosis remains strongly geography-linked in endemic regions and after travel or migration from endemic regions.

disease_course_modifier.trajectory_modulation: Delayed diagnosis or inadequate initial therapy increases chronic focal disease and relapse risk.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Brucellosis relapse is more likely after delayed or inadequate therapy.
Prolonged untreated bacteremia and intracellular persistence increase osteoarticular focal disease risk.
Delayed or incomplete treatment makes focal nidi more likely.

focal_complication_modifier.trajectory_modulation: Pre-existing valve/device/aneurysm disease redirects brucellosis toward endovascular focal infection, source-control need, and mortality.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Endocarditis is uncommon overall but enriched by abnormal valves, prosthetic valves, devices, and infected aneurysms.
Brucella endocarditis and infected aneurysm are major mortality pathways.
Endovascular brucellosis often needs valve, device, or aneurysm source control.

host_modifier.trajectory_modulation: Immunosuppression and poor host reserve can prolong intracellular survival, raise relapse risk, and worsen tolerance of focal disease.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Cell-mediated immunity is important for controlling intracellular Brucella.
Reduced host control can make eradication harder.
Poor physiologic reserve increases hazard from focal complications.

host_and_treatment_modifier.trajectory_modulation: Pregnancy changes antimicrobial feasibility and adds fetal risk outside the current lifespan-only outcome.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Pregnancy is a treatment-context modifier for brucellosis regimens.
Maternal mortality usually remains low with treatment, but severe maternal disease and fetal loss risk require special management.

treatment_modifier.trajectory_modulation: Renal impairment or dehydration mainly changes aminoglycoside safety and creatinine background rather than brucellosis probability.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Renal impairment increases aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity risk.
Baseline kidney disease shifts creatinine upward independently of brucellosis.

treatment_modifier.trajectory_modulation: Baseline hepatic disease or major drug interactions mainly change rifampin safety and liver-test interpretation.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Hepatic disease and interacting drugs increase rifampin-related risk.
Baseline liver disease can elevate AST independent of active brucellosis.

source_control_modifier.trajectory_modulation: Undrained abscess or retained infected hardware weakens antibiotic-only control and raises relapse.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Persistent focal nidus creates a direct source-control need.
Antibiotics are less definitive when an abscess or infected hardware remains.
Retained focal infection is a major relapse pathway.

supportive_care: Notify the microbiology laboratory when brucellosis is suspected because cultures require biosafety precautions and may need prolonged incubation.
Document exposure history explicitly: unpasteurized dairy, livestock contact, abattoir/veterinary/lab work, endemic residence/travel, hunting, and household cases.
Obtain blood cultures before antibiotics when feasible, but do not delay therapy in severe focal disease.
Use serology and repeat testing when early tests are negative but exposure plus syndrome remains compatible.

Screen for focal disease when symptoms point to it: MRI spine for persistent back/radicular pain, echocardiography for murmur/prosthetic valve/device/persistent bacteremia, lumbar puncture and MRI for neurologic signs, abdominal imaging for hepatosplenic pain or prolonged fever.
Monitor CBC, AST/ALT, bilirubin, creatinine, and inflammatory markers during prolonged therapy.
Assess adherence and drug interactions at each visit; relapse often reflects incomplete duration, monotherapy, or persistent focal nidus.
Coordinate source control with surgery, interventional radiology, neurosurgery, cardiology, or cardiac surgery when abscess, epidural extension, valve/device infection, or aneurysm is present.
Use antipyretics, hydration, nutrition support, and analgesia while antimicrobial therapy takes effect.
Public health counseling: avoid unpasteurized dairy and use occupational protective practices for livestock, abattoir, veterinary, and laboratory exposures.
quality_notes: No treatment ranking-label fields are used.
The only derived_hazard axis is mortality_hazard_in_D-BRUCELLOSIS.
Confirmatory microbiology axes are defined for ontology completeness; case files should place culture/speciation/serology/PCR in confirmatory_findings, not ordinary observations.
